content: Sodium benzoate, also known as benzoate of soda and labeled as E211, has the chemical formula NaC6H5CO2. It is the sodium salt of benzoic acid and exists in this form when dissolved in water. Sodium benzoate can be synthesized by reacting sodium hydroxide with benzoic acid. Sodium benzoate is widely used as a preservative due to its bacteriostatic and fungistatic properties under acidic conditions. It is commonly found in acidic foods such as salad dressings (containing vinegar), carbonated beverages (containing carbonic acid), jams and fruit juices (containing citric acid), pickles (containing vinegar), and various Chinese food sauces (such as soy, mustard, and duck sauces). Additionally, it is present in alcohol-based mouthwashes and silver polishes. On product labels, it is declared as sodium benzoate or E211. Interestingly, approximately 25% of the population cannot detect the taste of sodium benzoate, but for those who can, it may be perceived as sweet, sour, salty, or occasionally bitter. Sodium benzoate is also used in fireworks as a fuel in whistle mix, a powder that produces a whistling sound when compressed into a tube and ignited. Sodium benzoate occurs naturally in certain fruits and spices, including cranberries, prunes, greengage plums, cinnamon, ripe cloves, and apples. Organically grown cranberries and prunes may contain levels exceeding the typical 0.1% by weight. The International Programme on Chemical Safety has reported no adverse effects in humans at doses of 647–825 mg/kg of body weight per day. However, cats exhibit significantly lower tolerance to benzoic acid and its salts compared to rats and mice. The mechanism of sodium benzoate's food preservation begins with the absorption of benzoic acid into microbial cells. When the intracellular pH drops to 5 or lower, the anaerobic fermentation of glucose via phosphofructokinase is reduced by 95%, effectively inhibiting microbial growth. When combined with ascorbic acid (vitamin C, E300), sodium benzoate and potassium benzoate may form benzene, a known carcinogen. Factors such as heat, light, and shelf life can influence the rate of benzene formation. Professor Peter Piper from the University of Sheffield has raised concerns that sodium benzoate alone can damage and inactivate critical parts of mitochondrial DNA within cells. He explained that mitochondria are responsible for oxygen consumption and energy production, and damage to these structures can lead to severe cellular dysfunction. This mitochondrial damage has been linked to various diseases, including Parkinson's disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and the aging process. Research published in 2007 by the UK's Food Standards Agency (FSA) suggested a potential link between sodium benzoate (E211) and hyperactive behavior in children, as well as a decrease in intelligence. On September 6, 2007, the FSA issued updated guidance on certain artificial food additives, including sodium benzoate. Professor Jim Stevenson from Southampton University, the lead author of the study, stated that the research indicated an association between the consumption of specific mixtures of artificial food colors and sodium benzoate with increased hyperactivity in children. However, he cautioned that removing these additives from food alone would not prevent hyperactive disorders, as other factors also contribute to such behaviors. Two mixtures of additives were tested in the study: Mix A: Sunset yellow (E110), tartrazine (E102), carmoisine (E122), ponceau 4R (E124), and sodium benzoate (E211). Mix B: Sunset yellow (E110), quinoline yellow (E104), carmoisine (E122), allura red (E129), and sodium benzoate (E211). Sodium benzoate was included in both mixtures, but the observed effects on hyperactivity were inconsistent. The FSA concluded that if the observed increases in hyperactivity were real, they were more likely linked to one or more of the specific food colors tested rather than sodium benzoate itself. On April 10, 2008, the FSA called for the voluntary removal of these artificial colors (excluding sodium benzoate) by 2009. Additionally, it recommended phasing out these colors in food and beverages across the European Union over a specified period.
